consumers are willing (1) to spend more when they use a credit card versus when they use cash, (2) to spend less when they use cash versus when they use a gift certificate, (3) to spend more (less) when they use scrip (cash).
payment modes that differ in terms of form and/or payment coupling influence consumer spending behavior.
consumers spend more (vs. less) when they use credit cards (Study 1), scrip (Study 3), or gift certificates (Study 4) than cash.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of payment mode (cash, credit, scrip, and gift certificates) on consumer spending behavior and demonstrates that payment modes differ in terms that are important to consumer spending behavior.
the effect of payment mode on spending behavior.
the effects of payment coupling and physical form on consumer spending behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of payment mode is moderated by the degree to which consumers focus on the parting with money.
the effect of payment mode on spending is moderated by payment coupling and form.
the form in which money is paid influences consumer spending behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effect of payment mode is not simply a function of physical form but also the degree of payment coupling between the purchase decision and parting of the money.
payment coupling and form are both important determinants of consumer spending.
the form of money (i.e. cash vs. credit card) influences spending behavior, and this effect can be attenuate when consumers use a decomposition strategy to make their spending decision.
The main takeaway from our work is that

consumers spend more on a product when the product is paid for with a credit card versus cash or scrip, and that the effect of payment mode on spending can be attenuated through contextual manipulations that alter the salience of the parting with money.
consumers spend more money when the payment form (e.g., cash, credit card, or scrip) is salient in the context of a transaction.
consumers spend more with credit cards than cash, even when the two modes differ only in form.
